message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it looks different depending on a few key factors:

| Factor | Typical Effect on Color |
|--------|------------------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow water reflects the sky, so it can look light blue or even greenish‑white. Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange) and scatters shorter ones (blue, green), giving a deeper blue or indigo hue. |
| **Water Clarity** | Clear, clean water tends to be a vivid turquoise or deep blue. Turbid or muddy water can appear grayish or brownish. |
| **Algae & Phytoplankton** | High concentrations of green algae give the water a greenish tint; certain blooms can make it look almost green or even reddish. |
| **Sun Angle & Light** | A bright midday sun can make the sea sparkle with a bright, almost white‑blue sheen, while a low sun angle (sunrise/sunset) can cast warm orange or pink hues across the surface. |
| **Substrate** | Underlying sand, rocks, or coral can reflect light back into the water, altering its apparent color (e.g., sandy bottoms can give a warmer, yellowish tone). |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” it can range from pale turquoise to deep indigo, sometimes greenish or even brownish, depending on those conditions.
